prompt: You run `CREATE EXTENSION pgcrypto;` connected to the database `ana`. Where can `digest()` now be called?
hint: Compare what \dx showed in ana and in shop.

choices.text: In every database on the server, since the files are shared
choices.why: The files are shared; the objects are not. shop's \dx listed plpgsql and nothing else.

choices.text: In ana and in every database created from now on
choices.why: New databases copy template1, not ana. Only an extension created in template1 spreads that way.

choices.text: Only in sessions opened after a restart
choices.why: pgcrypto is not a preloaded library. Its library is loaded by a backend the first time a function needs it.

choices.text: In ana
choices.why: Right. The script ran inside ana, and the objects it created live in ana's catalogues alone.

prompt: `apt` has just upgraded the PostgreSQL package and replaced every file in `/usr/share/postgresql/16/extension`. What changed inside the databases that have pgcrypto installed?
hint: Which half of an extension does apt own?

choices.text: The objects were rebuilt from the new script at the next restart
choices.why: A restart reloads libraries, never SQL objects. The scripts run only on CREATE or ALTER EXTENSION.

choices.text: The extension was dropped and must be created again
choices.why: A package update never touches a database's catalogues; the extension is still recorded there.

choices.text: installed_version now matches default_version
choices.why: It is the other way round: default_version moved with the files, and installed_version stayed behind.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. The objects stay as CREATE EXTENSION made them until somebody runs ALTER EXTENSION … UPDATE.

prompt: A role `clerk` has CREATE on the database and is not a superuser. `CREATE EXTENSION pgcrypto` works for it and `CREATE EXTENSION pageinspect` is refused. What decides the difference?
hint: One line of the control file.

choices.text: `trusted = true` in pgcrypto's control file
choices.why: Right. A trusted extension may be created by any role with CREATE on the database; pageinspect is not trusted.

choices.text: pgcrypto was already installed in another database
choices.why: Each database is separate; an installation elsewhere grants nothing here.

choices.text: pageinspect needs shared_preload_libraries and a restart first
choices.why: The HINT said "Must be superuser to create this extension". It was a permission refusal, not a missing library.

choices.text: pgcrypto has no compiled library, so it carries no risk
choices.why: It does: pgcrypto.so sits in /usr/lib/postgresql/16/lib. Trust is declared, not inferred from having no C.

prompt: Match each file to what it does for pgcrypto.
hint: Name, objects, upgrade, code.

pairs.right: Says the default version, whether it is trusted, and where its library is
Holds the compiled code the functions call

prompt: A team wants pg_trgm available in every database the application will create from now on, without anybody remembering a command. What does that?
hint: Where does a new database come from?

choices.text: Adding pg_trgm to shared_preload_libraries
choices.why: That loads a library into processes; it creates no objects in any database.

choices.text: Creating it in the postgres database
choices.why: postgres is an ordinary database for connecting to. New databases copy template1.

choices.text: CREATE EXTENSION pg_trgm in template1
choices.why: Right. Every database created afterwards is a copy of template1 and carries the extension; existing ones still need it by hand.

choices.text: Installing the package again with apt
choices.why: The files are already there. Files on disk create nothing in a database.

prompt: After `CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements`, querying the view fails with "must be loaded via shared_preload_libraries". Why is CREATE EXTENSION not enough?
hint: Where does it keep its counts, and when is that sized?

choices.text: The extension needs a superuser to read the view
choices.why: ana is a superuser. The error names shared_preload_libraries, not a privilege.

choices.text: The view fills only after the next ANALYZE
choices.why: ANALYZE gathers table statistics for the planner. It has nothing to do with this view.

choices.text: It hooks every backend and keeps counts in shared memory sized at start
choices.why: Right. That can only be arranged when the server starts, so the library must be preloaded and the server restarted.

choices.text: A reload is needed after CREATE EXTENSION
choices.why: shared_preload_libraries has context postmaster: a reload marks it pending_restart and changes nothing.

prompt: `ALTER SYSTEM SET shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statement';` (one letter missing) answered ALTER SYSTEM. What happened at the restart, and how was it repaired?
hint: Can ALTER SYSTEM run with no server?

choices.text: It stayed down; postgresql.auto.conf was corrected by hand
choices.why: Right. With the server down there is nothing for ALTER SYSTEM to talk to, so the file it wrote is edited directly.

choices.text: The server skipped the unknown library and started with a warning
choices.why: It did not start: the log said FATAL, could not access file "pg_stat_statement", and pg_lsclusters said down.

choices.text: It stayed down; ALTER SYSTEM RESET repaired it
choices.why: ALTER SYSTEM needs a running server and a connection. Every connection was failing.

choices.text: ALTER SYSTEM should have refused the name, so the restart was fine
choices.why: ALTER SYSTEM checks only that the value is a list of names. Nothing reads it until the next start.

prompt: The workload ran `WHERE customer_id = :cid` with 200 random customers. Why is it one row in pg_stat_statements and not 200?
hint: Look at how the query text is shown.

choices.text: It keeps only the first execution of each query text
choices.why: calls says 200. Every execution was counted, under one row.

choices.text: pgbench sends one statement and repeats its result
choices.why: Each of the 200 runs reached the server and executed; the rows column counts all of them.

choices.text: pg_stat_statements.max is too small to hold 200 rows
choices.why: It holds 5000 distinct statements by default; 200 would have fitted easily.

choices.text: Constants are replaced by $1, so they share a shape
choices.why: Right. Statements are grouped by their shape after parsing, which is what makes the totals mean something.

prompt: Statement A runs 10 times a day at 2 s each. Statement B runs 2 million times a day at 1 ms each. Which leads pg_stat_statements ordered by total_exec_time, and what does that ordering tell you?
hint: Multiply first.

choices.text: A: it is the slowest, so improving it helps the server most
choices.why: A totals 20 s a day. The slowest call is what mean_exec_time ranks, not total.

choices.text: Neither; fast statements are left out of the view
choices.why: Every statement is counted, however fast. The customer lookup at a fraction of a millisecond was there.

choices.text: B, with 2000 s; that is where improving saves the server the most time
choices.why: Right. Total is calls times mean: 2,000,000 × 1 ms beats 10 × 2 s by a hundred to one.

choices.text: A, because pg_stat_statements weighs each call by its duration
choices.why: There is no weighting beyond adding up: total_exec_time is the plain sum of every call's time.

prompt: Why is `encode(digest(password, 'sha256'), 'hex')` a poor way to store passwords?
hint: Run it twice on one password, and time a hundred thousand.

choices.text: Same password, same hash, and it is very fast to compute
choices.why: Right. Equal passwords show as equal values, and a copy of the table can be tested at hundreds of thousands of guesses a second.

choices.text: SHA-256 can be decrypted with the right key
choices.why: A hash has no key and cannot be turned back. The weakness is elsewhere.

choices.text: Its output is too long for a text column
choices.why: 64 hexadecimal characters fit in text without trouble.

choices.text: digest is only available to superusers
choices.why: pgcrypto is trusted, and its functions are callable by ordinary roles.

prompt: At login, the typed password is checked with `password_hash = crypt(typed, ___)`, because the stored value carries its own salt and cost.
hint: The second argument of crypt is where it finds the salt.

prompt: A bcrypt hash made with `gen_salt('bf', 12)` costs how many times the work of one made with the default, cost 6?
hint: Each step up doubles the work.

prompt: An application inserts users with `crypt('…', gen_salt('bf'))` in its SQL. A DBA turns on `log_statement = 'all'` for an afternoon. What is now in the server log?
hint: What travels to the server inside the statement?

choices.text: Only the bcrypt values, since hashing happens before logging
choices.why: The statement is logged as it arrived, with the literal inside it; the hashing happens when it executes.

choices.text: Nothing, because statements with crypt are never logged
choices.why: There is no such exception. log_statement = 'all' means every statement.

choices.text: The salt alone, which is harmless
choices.why: gen_salt is called inside the statement; what the log holds is the statement's text, password included.

choices.text: Each new user's password, in plain text
choices.why: Right. The password is a literal in the statement, and log_statement writes the statement whole. Hashing in the application avoids it.

prompt: Why does the PostGIS package name, `postgresql-16-postgis-3`, carry the server's major version?
hint: Which server's directories does it fill?

choices.text: It is built for that one major version and installs into its directories
choices.why: Right. It serves 16 and nothing else; a 17 server needs postgresql-17-postgis-3.

choices.text: PostGIS is a contrib module released with each version
choices.why: It is a separate project with its own releases, which is why it was not in pg_available_extensions until installed.

choices.text: The number is the minimum version, and it runs on any later one
choices.why: A library compiled for 16 is not loaded by 17; each major version has its own package.

choices.text: It names the cluster, 16/main, that it will be created in
choices.why: A package creates nothing in any cluster. CREATE EXTENSION does that, per database.

prompt: `ST_Distance` between São Paulo and Rio answered 3.52 with `geometry` and 361 km with `geography`. What does 3.52 measure?
hint: geometry treats the coordinates as a flat plane.

choices.text: Hundreds of kilometres
choices.why: That would be 352 km, and the true distance is 361. The unit is not a distance on the ground at all.

choices.text: Miles, because geometry uses imperial units
choices.why: No unit of length is involved. 361 km is about 224 miles, nowhere near 3.52.

choices.text: Metres, with the points swapped by mistake
choices.why: Both queries used the same points in the same order. The type, not the input, changed the answer.

choices.text: Degrees on a flat drawing of the map
choices.why: Right. geometry takes longitude and latitude as x and y, so the straight line between them is in degrees.

prompt: A developer inserts Lisbon as `'POINT(38.7223 -9.1393)'`. What happens?
hint: Which number comes first in a PostGIS point?

choices.text: PostGIS rejects it because latitude must come first
choices.why: Longitude comes first, and both values are valid coordinates, so nothing is rejected.

choices.text: PostGIS detects the order and swaps them back
choices.why: It cannot know what was meant: 38.7 east, 9.1 south is a real place.

choices.text: It is stored without an error, far from Lisbon
choices.why: Right. The text is read as longitude 38.7, latitude -9.1, a point off the coast of East Africa, and every distance from it is wrong.

choices.text: It works, since geography ignores the order
choices.why: Order is the whole meaning: the first number is always x, the longitude.

prompt: pg_trgm shows `default_version` 1.6 and `installed_version` 1.5 in a database. What brings it to 1.6?
hint: The upgrade script is already on disk.

choices.text: Restarting the server so it loads the new files
choices.why: A restart reloads libraries. The SQL objects stay at 1.5 until an update is run.

choices.text: sudo apt install --reinstall postgresql-16
choices.why: The files already say 1.6; that is what default_version reports. The database is what lags.

choices.text: ALTER EXTENSION pg_trgm UPDATE
choices.why: Right. It runs pg_trgm--1.5--1.6.sql inside that database.

choices.text: Nothing; it updates itself at the next autovacuum
choices.why: Autovacuum cleans tables. Nothing updates an extension on its own.

prompt: The dump of `ana` was 112 lines though PostGIS alone had created 893 objects. What does that mean for the server that restores it?
hint: What did grep find in the dump?

choices.text: It needs nothing extra, since the dump is self-contained
choices.why: The 893 objects are not in it. Without the extension's files the CREATE EXTENSION line fails.

choices.text: It must restore with --schema-only first
choices.why: The flag changes what is dumped, not what the target needs. The missing piece is the package.

choices.text: It must already have the PostGIS package installed
choices.why: Right. The dump says CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS postgis, and that line needs the files on the new server.

choices.text: The dump has lost the PostGIS objects for good
choices.why: Nothing is lost: one line recreates all 893 from the extension's script, as long as the files are there.

prompt: Put the steps for carrying a PostGIS database through a major upgrade, 16 to 17, in order.
hint: The inventory comes first, the update of the objects last.
items: Run \dx in every database and list the extensions
Install postgresql-17-postgis-3 beside the new server
Run ALTER EXTENSION … UPDATE where installed and default differ
trap: Installing the package after the upgrade leaves the new server unable to create the extension the dump or the upgrade asks for.

prompt: On a managed service where you are never a superuser, which of these can you expect to install yourself, given CREATE on your database?
hint: Think of the trusted line, and of what needs more than a database.

choices.text: pgcrypto
choices.why: Right. It is trusted, so CREATE on the database is enough, the same as clerk had.

choices.text: pageinspect, to read raw pages
choices.why: It is not trusted: the lab refused it to clerk with "Must be superuser".

choices.text: pg_stat_statements, created and then enabled with ALTER SYSTEM
choices.why: ALTER SYSTEM and a restart are the provider's; preloading is a server setting you do not hold.

choices.text: Any extension at all, after installing its package with apt
choices.why: There is no shell on a managed server, so there is no apt; you choose among the files the provider installed.

prompt: A colleague wants pg_stat_statements on production and plans `ALTER SYSTEM SET shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements'` followed by a restart at 2 a.m. What one check costs a second and prevents the worst outcome?
hint: What made the lab server stay down?

choices.text: Run SELECT pg_reload_conf() and see whether it returns true
choices.why: The reload returns true whatever the value is; it reads nothing that only a start reads.

choices.text: Query pg_stat_statements first to see whether it is empty
choices.why: Before preloading, that query errors whatever the spelling in the setting.

choices.text: Run CREATE EXTENSION in template1 so the restart picks it up
choices.why: CREATE EXTENSION does not touch shared_preload_libraries, and the restart does not read template1.

choices.text: Check that pg_stat_statements.so exists in the library directory
choices.why: Right. A name with no matching library stops the server at start, and ls on the file catches a typo first.

prompt: Which of these change only files on disk and nothing inside any database? Choose all that apply.
hint: Separate the package's half from the database's half.

choices.text: sudo apt install -y postgresql-16-postgis-3
choices.why: Yes. It puts control files, scripts and libraries in place; no database has PostGIS until CREATE EXTENSION.

choices.text: CREATE EXTENSION pgcrypto
choices.why: That runs a script inside the current database and creates objects there.

choices.text: An apt upgrade of postgresql-16 that brings a new pg_trgm default
choices.why: Yes. default_version moves; installed_version stays where it was in every database.

choices.text: ALTER EXTENSION pg_trgm UPDATE
choices.why: That runs the upgrade script inside the database and changes its objects.

prompt: A new service needs random UUID primary keys and nothing else from pgcrypto. What is the leanest setup on PostgreSQL 16?
hint: Where did \df find gen_random_uuid?

choices.text: CREATE EXTENSION pgcrypto in the service's database
choices.why: That was needed before 13. Now it adds an extension to carry through upgrades for no gain.

choices.text: CREATE EXTENSION "uuid-ossp" instead of pgcrypto
choices.why: Another extension for the same job; the server already has the function.

choices.text: Generate UUIDs with digest(random()::text, 'md5')
choices.why: That is a hash of a weak random number shaped by hand, and it still needs pgcrypto.

choices.text: No extension: gen_random_uuid() is core
choices.why: Right. It lives in pg_catalog since PostgreSQL 13, and shop, with no pgcrypto, called it.

hint: Statistics, passwords, places, text.

pairs.right: Finding which statements take the server's time
Storing a password as a salted bcrypt hash
Distances between points on the Earth
